pending_articles.title: Human iEEG recordings during audiovisual speech violations support and extend predictive routing models
pending_articles.content: Rather than constantly reconstructing the world solely through sensory input, predictive processing theories posit that the brain utilizes predictions maintained as internal representations to guide sensory processing. An emerging model, predictive routing, proposes that an interplay between neuronal gamma (40-150 Hz) and alpha-beta (10-30 Hz) rhythms implements a dynamic mechanism for predictive processing. Namely, predictions enhance alpha-beta oscillations that suppress gamma activity during the processing of predicted inputs. While this model is supported by animal studies, its validity has not been fully explored within the human brain. The present study addresses this by leveraging human intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings across superior temporal and prefrontal/premotor areas of seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm. We calculated iEEG power in the theta, alpha-beta, and high gamma bands during simple auditory deviance, multisensory integration, and a condition where an incongruent visual cue (lip movements) clashed with an auditory stimulus (a syllable), creating audiovisual incongruence that can elicit the McGurk illusion. Results revealed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power in the superior temporal cortex in response to auditory deviance and the McGurk condition, while frontal areas, despite reflecting a similar decrease in alpha-beta power, did not present this high gamma prediction error signal. Instead, the theta band revealed a strong prediction error signal in the McGurk condition, consistent with theories on the role of theta in reorganizing cortical networks. These results both support and extend existing predictive routing models for human-specific forms of predictive processing.

pending_articles.title: The human-specific gene FRMPD2B couples postnatal experience to the expansion of cortical connectivity
pending_articles.content: The human neocortex is characterized by its uniquely prolonged postnatal developmental period during which experience sculpts neuronal circuits, a process essential to human cognitive abilities. Yet whether human-specific genetic innovations have shaped the activity-dependent mechanisms regulating circuit assembly remains unknown. Here, we identify the human-specific gene FRMPD2B as an activity- and experience-regulated modifier of cortical connectivity. FRMPD2B is primarily expressed in cortico-cortical projection neurons postnatally and throughout childhood. It promotes dendritic, axonal and synaptic development, and is required for proper morphogenesis in xenotransplanted human cortical neurons. FRMPD2B expression is bidirectionally regulated by neuronal activity and experience. This activity-responsiveness was gained after FRMPD2B arose through partial gene duplication, when a retrotransposon insertion remodeled its promoter. Our findings highlight how a series of genetic innovations have led to the emergence of a human-specific activity-regulated developmental program through which postnatal experience drives cortical connectivity expansion, linking genome evolution to human brain plasticity.

pending_articles.title: Superior Frontal Gyrus Cortical Thickness Mediates the Association Between Openness to Experience and Theory of Mind: Evidence from the Human Connectome Project
pending_articles.content: Background: Theory of mind (ToM), the capacity to infer the mental states of others, varies considerably across healthy adults. Openness to experience has been linked both to social-cognitive abilities and to thinner prefrontal cortex, but whether cortical structure statistically accounts for the association between openness and ToM is unknown. We tested whether bilateral superior frontal gyrus (SFG) cortical thickness mediates this association. Methods: Data from 1,049 healthy young adults with complete data were drawn from the Human Connectome Project. ToM was indexed by accuracy on the Heider-Simmel social animation task, openness by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and SFG thickness by FreeSurfer. Models adjusted for age, sex, intracranial volume and fluid intelligence; indirect effects were tested with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied. Results: Openness showed a positive total effect on ToM accuracy (beta = .081, p = .009). Higher openness was associated with thinner left and right SFG (beta = -.085 and -.084), and thinner SFG with higher ToM accuracy (beta = -.082 and -.075). Indirect effects were significant (left: .0069, 95% CI [.0010, .0158]; right: .0063, 95% CI [.0007, .0146]), accounting for approximately 8.5% and 7.8% of the total effect, and remained significant after rank-based normalisation of the ceiling-affected ToM scores. Conclusions: SFG cortical thickness partially and statistically mediates the association between openness to experience and social cognition. Because the data are cross-sectional and effects are small, the findings do not establish a causal mechanism, neural efficiency or synaptic pruning, but they identify a candidate structural pathway for longitudinal testing.

pending_articles.title: A Unified World Model in Human Posterior Parietal Cortex
pending_articles.content: How does the brain understand the physical world, predict future events, and plan actions? Are these problems solved by a unified world model, as hypothesized by cognitive scientists and artificial intelligence researchers? Posterior parietal cortex has been implicated in all these functions, but whether the same neurons support each of them is unknown. We recorded from the superior parietal lobule (SPL) of two tetraplegic participants implanted with microelectrode arrays. SPL units preferentially engaged by intuitive physics, judging block-tower stability and viewing naturalistic physical events, also predicted whether moving objects would collide hundreds of milliseconds before contact, generalizing between different physical scenarios. These populations also encoded which hand action the participant intended to perform. These findings identify SPL as a substrate for physical world modeling.

pending_articles.title: Cortical long-range dynamics track excitation-inhibition balance across cognitive states and organizational principles
pending_articles.content: A fundamental question in systems neuroscience is how the brain's excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance shapes the temporal structure of neural activity and whether we can non-invasively recover this relationship from neural scaling properties. We show that MRS-derived E/I balance is expressed in long-range temporal dynamics and constrained by cytoarchitecture. The laminar organisation of inhibitory circuits, spanning agranular to granular cortex, determines how faithfully regional dynamics reflect E/I balance. This neurochemical signature is state-dependent: its relationship with cortical dynamics reverses during task engagement, consistent with traversal of dynamical regimes around a critical point. It extends beyond fMRI to arousal-linked dynamics, indexed by pupil diameter and microsaccades, indicating a global mode of cortical state rather than a regionally isolated property. The imprint of E/I balance on long-range dynamics follows the sensory-association axis at rest, and is reconfigured during task engagement. These findings establish E/I balance as a neurochemical quantity with structured, scalable signatures across the temporal and spatial organization of the human cortex.

Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding
pending_articles.content: Objective. Speech brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a pivotal technology in facilitating communication for individuals with speech impairments. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) for noninvasive speech BCIs offers an accessible and affordable solution, potentially benefiting a broader audience. However, EEG-based speech decoding remains controversial especially for overt speech, due to difficulties in separating speech-related neural activities from myoelectric potential artifacts generated during articulation. Moreover, because paradigms for collecting covert speech data are inherently less scalable than those for overt speech, whether the neural dynamics underlying EEG-based decoding of overt speech are also present during covert speech remains an open and practically important question. Approach. Here we aim to delineate the extent of the neural contributions to EEG-based speech decoding, and the degree to which the underlying neural dynamics are shared across overt and covert speech, by employing Explainable AI techniques to a convolutional neural network predicting spoken words based on signals obtained by ultra-high-density (uhd)-EEG. Main results. We found that electrode-wise contributions to the decoding cannot be explained by their mutual information with electromyography (EMG). Furthermore, contributing periods of speech to EEG-based decoding are distinct from those to decoding solely relying on EMG. Contributing periods of EEG-based decoding partially overlapped between overt and minimally overt speech. Notably, the denoising process successfully enhanced the decoding contribution from electrodes within speech-related brain areas for all speech conditions. Significance. Altogether, our findings support the idea that, with appropriate preprocessing, EEG becomes a valuable tool for decoding spoken words based on underlying neural activities.

pending_articles.title: Diff-ADN: a diffusion-guided artifact denoising network with deterministic residual refinement for EEG
pending_articles.content: Objective. Physiological artifacts degrade electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings and can affect downstream brain–computer interface (BCI) analysis. This study develops a compact single-channel framework for ocular, muscular, cardiac, and mixed-artifact removal. Approach. The Diffusion-Guided Artifact Denoising Network (Diff-ADN) employs a two-stage framework comprising severity-conditioned Stage-I reconstruction followed by diffusion-guided Stage-II residual refinement. During training, forward noising and velocity prediction supervise the Stage-II encoder, whereas inference requires only a single deterministic residual correction, without iterative reverse-diffusion sampling. The framework was evaluated under contamination levels ranging from to dB, using independently recorded artifact sources and motor-imagery decoding across four public EEG datasets. Main results. Diff-ADN achieved mean Pearson correlations of 0.936, 0.839, 0.886, and 0.844 for electrooculographic (EOG),electromyographic (EMG), electrocardiographic (ECG), and mixed EOG+EMG artifacts, respectively. When tested with independently recorded artifact sources, performance varied by artifact type: larger reductions were observed for EOG and EMG, while PTB and INCART ECG differed from the MIT–BIH reference by 0.026 and 0.014, respectively. Across the four motor-imagery datasets, ECG denoising recovered 4.88–5.59 percentage points (pp) in decoding accuracy compared with artifact-corrupted EEG. The largest recovery was 21.90 pp for PTB ECG artifacts on BCI IV-2a at dB. Significance. The proposed framework combines artifact-aware EEG reconstruction with efficient deterministic inference, processing 2 s segments in 12.52–17.08 ms on the tested CPU. Results across independent artifact sources and multiple motor-imagery datasets further show that improvements in waveform reconstruction do not necessarily translate into uniform recovery of BCI decoding accuracy.

recently_processed.title: New software package: ERPLAB Studio
recently_processed.content:
We are excited to announce the release of a new EEG/ERP analysis package, ERPLAB Studio. We think it’s a huge improvement over the classic EEGLAB user interface. See our cheesy “advertisement” video to get a quick overview.

Rather than operating as an EEGLAB plugin, ERPLAB Studio is a standalone Matlab program that provides a more efficient and user-friendly interface to the most commonly used EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines.

With ERPLAB Studio, you automatically see the EEG or ERP waveforms as soon as you load a file. And as soon as you perform an operation, you see what the new EEG/ERP looks like. For example, when you filter the data, you immediately see the filtered waveforms.

You can even select multiple datasets and apply an operation like artifact detection on all of them in one step. And then you can immediately see the results, such as which EEG epochs have been marked with artifacts.

We give you access to EEGLAB’s ICA-based artifact correction tools, but with a nice bonus. You can plot the ICA activations in the same window with the EEG data, making it easy to see which ICA components correspond to specific artifacts such as eyeblinks.

The program has an EEG tab for processing continuous and epoched EEG data, and an ERP tab for processing averaged ERPs.

The automatic ERP plotting makes it easy for you to view the data laid out according to the electrode locations. And we have an Advanced Waveform Viewer that can make publication-quality plots.

ERPLAB Studio is mainly just a new user interface. Under the hood, we’re running the same EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines you’ve always used. And scripting is identical.

ERPLAB Studio is included in version 11 and higher of ERPLAB. You simply follow our download/installation instructions and then type estudio from the Matlab command line.

If you’re new to ERPLAB, we strongly recommend that you go through our tutorial before starting to process your own data.

If you already know how to use the original version of ERPLAB (which we now call ERPLAB Classic), you can quickly learn how to use ERPLAB Studio with our Transition Guide.

We also have a manual that describes every feature in detail.

recently_processed.title: Automated multiscale high-content imaging connects plaque population heterogeneity to localized synapse loss
recently_processed.content: Synapse loss is a major correlate of cognitive decline in neurodegenerative disease, yet its relationship to localized pathology remains difficult to study at scale. Conventional confocal imaging approaches are limited by low throughput, selection bias, and restricted sampling of pathological features. Here, we describe an automated high-content imaging and analysis workflow that enables large-scale quantification of amyloid beta plaque-associated synapse loss within mouse brain tissue. Using Preciscan-based multiscale acquisition on the Opera Phenix platform, this workflow combines tissue-wide pathology mapping with targeted high-magnification imaging and subcellular analysis. We apply this framework to acquire and analyze hundreds of plaque images in the CRND8 mouse model of A{beta} proteinopathy, demonstrating plaque-associated synapse loss within developing plaque populations over disease progression. We find that small diffuse plaques accumulate rapidly at late stages in CRND8, but that the primary synapse loss comes from large cored plaques. More broadly, this scalable framework enables systematic investigation of subcellular phenomena across pathological microenvironments in disease models.

recently_processed.title: The Canadian Pediatric Imaging Platform (C-PIP) Reference Sample: Neuroimaging Protocol and Cross-site Validation for Harmonized Multimodal Pediatric Imaging
recently_processed.content: Understanding how the human brain matures from infancy through adolescence is essential for identifying factors that influence health outcomes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides powerful tools for characterizing structural, microstructural, functional, and metabolic aspects of brain development; however, many pediatric imaging studies are constrained by small sample sizes, limited geographic diversity, lack of longitudinal measurement, restricted age ranges, and heterogeneous acquisition protocols. While recent large-scale neuroimaging consortia have begun to address these challenges, such resources remain limited in the Canadian context, creating a critical gap. The Canadian Pediatric Imaging Platform (C-PIP) has developed a multisite neuroimaging framework across three of Canada's largest pediatric hospitals: Alberta Children's Hospital (Calgary), Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Sainte-Justine (Montreal), and the Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto). These three sites were united through a national initiative, leveraging high-performance MRI systems to accelerate Canadian neurodevelopmental research. In addition, C-PIP has implemented a centralized data sharing infrastructure to facilitate open science and collaborative research across institutions. Here, we describe the development and implementation of a multimodal MRI acquisition protocol designed to support multimodal longitudinal studies of typical and atypical brain development spanning infancy through adolescence. Within-site stability and cross-site stability of C-PIP core MRI sequences were evaluated using a travelling-participant study. The C-PIP MRI protocol establishes a harmonized, multisite imaging framework that supports large-scale investigations of pediatric brain development and disorders.

recently_processed.title: Recurrent Spiking Neural Networks for Continuous Motor Control: A Biologically Plausible Model of Motor Cortex
recently_processed.content: Motor cortex acquires skilled movements through recurrent spiking dynamics and experience-dependent synaptic plasticity, yet how such circuits learn continuous motor control using biologically local signals remains unclear. Here, we develop a recurrent spiking neural network model of motor cortex that addresses both the computational and biological requirements of motor learning. We first analytically derived the recurrent firing-rate state directly from synaptic input and trained the network by implicit differentiation, thereby avoiding backpropagation through long spike trajectories. We then introduced State-Carry Initialization, which enables closed-loop motor control by continuously carrying the ongoing recurrent state across successive actions. Building on this formulation, we devised a learning rule termed Feedback-Spike Nudging (FSN), in which teaching signals are delivered as spikes through a feedback pathway. Synaptic changes depend only on presynaptic activity and the feedback-evoked change in postsynaptic firing, consistent with biological mechanisms of synaptic plasticity in motor cortex. The resulting networks learned continuous motor control through both supervised and reinforcement learning, which could be mapped respectively onto interactions of motor cortex with the cerebellum and basal ganglia. Moreover, the FSN learning rule was consistent with experimental observations of structural spine plasticity in mouse motor cortex. Thus, our study lays a foundation for recurrent spiking models of motor cortex that are biologically grounded at both the functional and anatomical levels.
